content: The prevention and control of HIV infections, as well as the epidemiology of HIV and AIDS, are critical areas of focus in global health. Efforts to address these issues are supported by national health programs, strategic health planning, and guidelines developed by organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO). This guide aims to assist countries in planning and managing program reviews to assess and improve the health sector's response to HIV. It complements previous WHO guidance on strategic and operational planning for HIV/AIDS and builds on other thematic or regional program review guidelines. The guide does not prescribe a specific approach but instead outlines general principles and processes for conducting program reviews. These reviews help evaluate program results and implementation effectiveness, primarily within the health sector under the stewardship of the Ministry of Health. Elements of the guide can also be applied to multisectoral reviews of national AIDS responses. The guide is divided into two parts. The first part describes the principles and processes for reviewing programs, including preparation, planning, data collection, analysis, synthesis, dissemination, and use of findings. The second part provides checklists of key review questions for major intervention areas, which can be adapted to various contexts and purposes. These questions can also aid in developing data collection tools such as questionnaires and observation checklists. The primary audience for this guide includes national HIV program managers and officers responsible for planning and monitoring in health ministries. It is also intended for other government, nongovernmental, private-sector, and international partners involved in planning, implementing, and funding HIV programs at different levels of the health system. Significant progress has been made in the global response to the AIDS epidemic since the early 2000s. The number of people receiving antiretroviral treatment has increased dramatically, and prevention efforts have led to a steady decline in new HIV infections worldwide. Development assistance for HIV and health has grown, and many lowand middle-income countries are increasing their national funding for HIV programs. However, challenges remain in achieving the goal of zero new HIV infections, zero AIDS-related deaths, and zero HIV-related stigma and discrimination. Progress is not uniform across all countries, with some experiencing increases or resurgences in new infections and low treatment coverage in certain regions. In light of these challenges and opportunities, HIV programs must adopt more strategic designs and smarter implementation to meet ambitious global and national commitments. Programs should define clear priorities based on evidence, allocate resources accordingly, implement interventions at sufficient scale, and continuously evaluate their effectiveness. Regular program reviews are integral to the program cycle, aiming to improve performance and achieve better results. The health sector plays a central role in the national response to HIV, delivering essential services such as antiretroviral therapy, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, male circumcision, HIV testing, harm reduction, and services for key affected populations. It also conducts HIV surveillance, manages health commodities, and undertakes research and evaluation. A strong health sector HIV program contributes to a robust national AIDS response. In some countries, the health sector leads all HIV efforts, while in others, coordination is managed by separate bodies such as national AIDS commissions. Program reviews are systematic assessments of a program's performance over a defined period. They are a form of monitoring that provides feedback to inform planning and improve implementation. Monitoring involves routine tracking and reporting on program progress and performance, while evaluation rigorously analyzes program outcomes and the factors influencing them. Program reviews use information from monitoring, evaluation, and other sources to determine whether programs are on track and achieving desired results. Regular program reviews are considered best practices in managing HIV programs. They help improve program results, enhance efficiency, strengthen accountability, foster partnerships, and mobilize resources. Reviews can be conducted at different stages of the program cycle, including annual, mid-term, and end-term reviews, as well as specific thematic or project reviews. Each type of review serves distinct purposes, such as assessing progress, making adjustments, or evaluating overall performance and impact. A comprehensive program review should cover the full spectrum of program results, from inputs to impact. It should address key questions such as whether the right interventions are being implemented, whether they are being delivered effectively and at scale, whether the right populations are being reached, and whether the program is making a measurable difference. These questions align with the main domains of monitoring and evaluation, including inputs, processes, outputs, outcomes, and impact. In summary, program reviews are essential tools for improving the performance and impact of HIV programs. By conducting regular and systematic reviews, countries can strengthen their health sector responses to HIV and contribute to achieving global health goals.
